newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels might leave Peru under deal - sources.
newsitem.headline: Rebels might leave Peru under deal - sources.

text.p: Peru's hostage-takers would accept asylum in Cuba and might take some of their 72 captives with them as guarantors under a draft accord to end the 14-week standoff in Lima, diplomatic sources said on Tuesday.

Other parts of the deal have yet to be negotiated, a process that could take a couple of weeks, the diplomats said. But for the first time in the 98-day standoff momentum was building for a deal to free the hostages and let their captors take up a Caribbean exile, they said.

"There really is a certain degree of optimism," Bolivia's acting ambassador, Eloy Avila, told local Radio Programas. "We see flexibility on the part of the government and the MRTA," he said. Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio is one of the hostages.

The main obstacle now is the demand by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels for freedom for hundreds of jailed comrades -- a demand rejected by President Alberto Fujimori, diplomatic sources said.
"Asylum seems to be pretty well sewn up," said one diplomat. "The core issue now is what to do about the prisoners. That's the real area of contention."

Cuba and the Dominican Republic have offered asylum as long as it forms part of an overall settlement to the siege, in which 72 men are being held by the rebels in a house with no electricity or running water.

The rebels initially spurned asylum, saying they preferred to return to armed struggle after winning release of their comrades, but have since said they could accept asylum for at least some of their number.

"For a long time the talks seemed to be going up and down every day. But now there's progress, there's a mood of optimism," one diplomat said, cautioning that even if talks went smoothly from now on freedom for hostages could be 10 days to two weeks away.
Another diplomatic source said the MRTA wanted to take a handful of its top hostages to the Caribbean on board its asylum flight.
Despite the most positive mood in Lima for weeks, there was no confirmation from official quarters that a deal was close.

President Alberto Fujimori, inaugurating a scenic viewing point on a Lima hilltop, made no specific reference to the crisis negotiations but called for a "rational solution" and pledged "solidarity" with the hostages.
"May Holy Week be propitious so that respect for peace, life and liberty is imposed. That is what Peru wants," he said.

In the latest of a flurry of meetings, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, both guarantors, met the MRTA command on Tuesday first inside the residence and then at a safe house outside.
The meeting was also attended by Japanese government observer Terusuke Terada. But all parties left afterward without comment to the waiting horde of journalists.
A press officer for the Japanese government's delegation in Lima said Tokyo had no official comment on the rumours.
Asylum is part of the draft deal hammered out by a three-man mediation team after talks with both sides, sources said.

"All this does not mean we are at the doorstep of a solution but it does mean we have reached a road that will take us to a solution," Ambassador Avila said. "We hope that with the next conversations starting on Monday or Tuesday we will have something to celebrate."
